narrative:
The model predicted a 63.4% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. Being in the bottom decile (1 out of 10) is substantially lower than the average ranking of accepted students (around 5.8), signaling that your later-year performance raised serious concerns about readiness for the bar. Your first-year ranking was the second most important factor and also pulled the prediction toward failure; your decile of 2 compared with an average of 6 among accepted students reinforced the pattern of lower academic standing.

Your family income bracket worked in the opposite direction. Coming from an upper-middle income background slightly favored passing, consistent with the fact that most accepted students also come from similar or higher brackets. However, this positive influence was not large enough to overcome the academic signals.

Taken together, the model concluded that your lower class rankings in both early and later years created too high a risk of bar exam failure. To improve your chances, you should focus on raising your academic performance, consider retaking courses or additional bar-preparation work, and then reapply once you have stronger evidence of improvement.
